transcript.text: Our Henry has gone a bit weak and sounds rough, sort of rattly growl instead of the normal hum. It's about 12 years old. Bags and filter are new. Worth fixing?

Usually yes. Henrys are simple, sturdy machines and very repairable. Even a replacement motor is normally well worth fitting compared with buying new, and a good repairer can often do it cheaply. A 12-year-old Henry with a fresh motor can easily go on for years more. With a new bag and filter it's still weak and sounds rough, so I'd put a worn motor at the top of the list. A growl or rattle instead of the normal hum is typical of tired motor bearings or carbon brushes worn right down. The main thing to rule out first is a blockage or something rattling in the airway, because that can also cause weak suction and an odd note. 1. Unplug it, take the hose off and look through it. Do the same with the wands. A coin dropped through should fall straight out. Check the floor tool's neck too, and squeeze along the hose for splits or hard lumps. If you find a blockage or split, that's likely your answer.
2. Make sure the bag is fitted properly on the inlet and the motor head clips down evenly on the tub. A gap leaks air and kills suction.
3. Plug it back in with the hose off and run it for a few seconds while you listen. If it still growls and rattles with nothing attached, the noise is coming from the motor itself. If the noise is still there with the hose off, it's probably the motor (bearings or brushes). That's a job for a vacuum repair shop, or for a confident DIYer, as the head has to come apart. Stop using it heavily in the meantime. Worn brushes can arc and damage the motor further, and a seizing bearing can overheat. If you smell burning or see sparks through the vents, stop using it straight away.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — Lost suction is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage in the hose, tube or floor head — check and clear those before suspecting the motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

Thank you. The coin goes straight through the hose, and the bag and filter are fitted correctly (genuine bag, new cloth filter last week). Now that you mention it, there is a hot, burning electrical smell after about five minutes, and when I looked at the vents on top in the dark hall I saw sparks flickering inside. Should I stop using it?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Yes, stop using it now and keep it unplugged. Don't use it again until a vacuum repairer has checked it. What you're describing fits the motor. The most likely cause is carbon brushes worn right down. They then arc heavily against the commutator, which is the sparking and the smell you're getting. The bearings are probably tired too, which gives the growl. Every extra run risks scorching the commutator or windings, so stopping now gives the best chance that a simple motor swap will sort it. It's still very much worth repairing. On a 12-year-old Henry, a vacuum repair shop will usually fit a replacement motor, and it's normally well worth it against buying new. The rest of the machine is simple and long-lasting. To help find the right motor, could you tell me the model number? It's on the rating label, which is usually on the body, often on the underside or back of the motor head. It can wait if it's awkward to find right now.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Thank you, I'll stop using it and leave it unplugged. The label on the bottom says HVR 200-22. Is that what you need?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes, that's exactly what's needed. HVR 200-22 reads like a model from Numatic's Henry range. That label is what a repairer will use to match the right replacement motor. They'll confirm the exact version when they see it, so take a photo of the label or bring the machine along. Add the sparking and burning smell, and the motor is the clear culprit. I'm fairly confident it's worn carbon brushes arcing on the commutator, with tired bearings causing the growl. There's nothing more for you to check at home, and it shouldn't be run again until a repairer has looked at it. 1. Keep it unplugged and take it, with the hose, to a local vacuum repair shop. Many service Henrys routinely.
2. Tell them about the sparking, the burning smell after about five minutes, and the rattly growl. That points them straight at the motor.
3. Ask for a quote before they start. On many motors like this the brushes aren't sold separately, so a whole replacement motor is often the practical fix. On a Henry that's usually still well worth it against buying new. If they find scorching beyond the motor itself, such as damaged wiring or the switch, they'll tell you. Even then, these machines are simple enough that repair normally still makes sense.
